verses.text: But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine.
Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance.
Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.
In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children,
to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited.
In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled.
In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity,
and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us.
Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative,
not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.
It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.
Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

context.author: Paul the apostle (1:1)
context.audience: Titus, Paul’s coworker, left in Crete
context.setting: Paul tells Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine. He gives instructions for older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. All are grounded in the gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all, training us to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
context.custom: This is a household code, like those in Ephesians and Colossians. Ancient writers warned that Christians threatened social order, so Paul tells them to live so that “the word of God may not be reviled.” Paul calls the church “a people for his own possession,” echoing Israel.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 3 widens the instructions to society and ends with warnings and greetings.
context.timelineBible: “A people for his own possession” (v.14) recalls Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6, 14:2. The idea of redemption from lawlessness echoes Psalm 130:8.
context.sparkNotes: Teach what accords with sound doctrine: older men should be sober and dignified, older women reverent and able to teach younger women, younger men self-controlled. Slaves should be trustworthy and adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and training us to renounce ungodliness and wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us.

translation.meaning: To shine upon. It was used of the arrival of a god or king.
To buy back from slavery for a price.

overview.summary: Every age and group is to live out sound teaching. The grace of God trains us to live self-controlled, upright lives as we wait for the appearing of Jesus Christ.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes to Titus, who is in Crete.

history.t: Greek writers such as Aristotle set out the duties of each person in a household. Titus 2:1-10 gives short duties for older men and women, younger women and men, and slaves, and ties each to the gospel: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5) and so that slaves may adorn the teaching about God our Savior (2:10).

Paul says the grace of God “has appeared” (2:11) and looks for the “glorious appearance” of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13). The Greek word epiphaneia was used in the Greek world for the arrival of a ruler or a god’s help. Antiochus IV took the title Epiphanes, “God Manifest.”

customs.t: Slaves are to “adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (2:10). The Greek verb kosmeo means to put in order or to decorate, and it is also used for jewelry and dress (1 Peter 3:5). Slaves with no say in their circumstances are called to make the gospel attractive by honest, faithful work.

Christ gave Himself “to redeem us from all lawlessness” (2:14). The Greek verb is from the word family for a ransom price paid to free a captive or a slave. The Old Testament uses the idea for God’s freeing Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8).

archaeology.t: The Law Code of Gortyn is a long Greek inscription of the early 5th century BC, about 500 years before Titus. Its rules cover marriage, divorce, property, inheritance and slaves. The Roman Odeion at Gortyn was built around it. It shows how Cretans ordered family life long before Paul, but Titus does not refer to it.

Roman houses with mosaics and painted walls have been dug at Knossos and Gortyn. Most of what survives is from the 2nd century AD or later, after Paul. They show what a well-off household on the island looked like, but the letter does not describe any house.

overview.discussion: Paul says the grace of God trains us. In what area of my life is grace teaching me to say no and yes?
overview.book: The letter to Titus · 3 chapters. Short, practical instructions for a church on a difficult island.
overview.author: Paul
